questions.question: Define natural resources, distinguish between renewable and non-renewable resources with two examples each, and name two of South Africa's natural resource strengths and one weakness.
questions.expected_answer: Natural resources (land) are gifts of nature used in production: land, soil, water, minerals, forests, fish, sunlight, wind. Renewable: can be replaced naturally if used wisely — sunlight, wind, forests, fish, rainwater, well-managed soil. Non-renewable: fixed amounts, cannot be replaced — coal, gold, platinum, oil, gas. Strengths: large reserves of platinum, manganese, chrome, gold and coal; excellent sunshine and wind for renewable energy; long coastline. Weakness: water scarcity and little land suitable for crops.

questions.question: Name the four factors of production and their remuneration. A farm's income is R500 000; it pays rent R60 000, wages R220 000 and interest R30 000. Calculate the profit, and the result if income falls to R280 000.
questions.expected_answer: Natural resources — rent; labour — wages and salaries; capital — interest; entrepreneurship — profit. Profit = 500 000 − 60 000 − 220 000 − 30 000 = R190 000. With income R280 000: costs = 60 000 + 220 000 + 30 000 = R310 000; 280 000 − 310 000 = −R30 000, a loss borne by the entrepreneur because profit is the residual after all other factors are paid.

questions.question: Explain how the remuneration of the factors of production links businesses and households in the circular flow, and why the distribution of factor income affects inequality.
questions.expected_answer: Households own the factors of production and supply them to businesses in the factor market (real flow); businesses pay rent, wages and salaries, interest and profit to households (money flow — factor income). Households spend this income on goods and services in the goods and services market, and businesses use that revenue to pay for factors again. If ownership of land and capital and access to skills and jobs are concentrated, most factor income goes to a few households while others receive little and rely on grants, increasing inequality; broader ownership, skills and employment spread factor income more widely.
